local_calendar.t: On November 3, 2026 the voters of Maryland's 23 counties and of Baltimore City elect county officers to four-year terms: the State Board's list has contests for state's attorney, clerk of the circuit court, register of wills and sheriff in all 24, a county council or county commissioners in 23, a county executive in 8, judges of the orphans' court in 21 and a treasurer in 3, and members of 23 boards of education are chosen on the nonpartisan part of the same ballot. Baltimore City elects its mayor and city council in presidential years, next in 2028. The other cities and towns run their own elections under their charters, apart from the State Board's; Cumberland's mayor and council are the one city contest on its November list.

measures.t: Arbitration Reform for State Employees Act of 2026
measures.q:
Providing that each budget submitted by the Governor shall include proposed expenditures necessary to implement wages, hours, fringe benefits, health benefits, and other terms and conditions of employment in each collective bargaining memorandum of understanding with State employees, whether the State and State employees reached those terms and conditions by mutual agreement or through a neutral decider's order.
(Amending Article III of the Maryland Constitution)
measures.y: A vote FOR this amendment means that the Governor has to include money in the proposed State budget to pay for agreements between the State and its employees. Agreements might include changes to wages, hours, fringe benefits, health benefits, and other terms and conditions of employment. The Governor must put enough money in the State budget to cover the agreed upon pay and benefits for employees, whether those terms were negotiated or decided by a neutral decision-maker.
measures.no: A vote AGAINST the amendment means that the law about funding agreements between the State and State employees stays the same.
measures.r: To pass, the amendment needs more FOR votes than AGAINST votes among the votes cast on it. (Maryland Constitution, article XIV, section 1)
measures.h: Proposed by the General Assembly in Chapter 155 of 2026 (House Bill 604). In Maryland an amendment is proposed by a bill passed by three-fifths of all the members elected to each house and then goes to the voters at the next general election (Maryland Constitution, article XIV, section 1); there is no citizen initiative for amendments.
measures.nt: The ballot heads this question "Constitutional Amendment (Ch. 155 of the 2026 Legislative Session)" and prints the two statements of what each vote does beside the choices "For the Constitutional Amendment" and "Against the Constitutional Amendment". The question and those statements are the Secretary of State's wording as the State Board of Elections posted it after public comment (updated August 4, 2026); the Allegany County specimen ballot, looked at as a sample, prints the statements under the question.

measures.t: Temporary Appointments on the Commission on Judicial Disabilities
measures.q:
Authorizing temporary substitute appointments to the Commission on Judicial Disabilities when a member is recused or disqualified, or when a member's term expires. In these situations, the Commission Chair may recall a former member of the Commission, or the Governor, at the request of the Commission Chair, may appoint a temporary substitute member or extend the term of a current member until a permanent replacement is appointed. Only individuals who meet the constitutional eligibility requirements may be recalled or appointed to the Commission.
(Amending Article IV of the Maryland Constitution)
measures.y: A vote FOR this amendment means that temporary appointments to the Commission are allowed if a member is recused, disqualified, or if a member's term ends without a replacement. The Commission Chair can temporarily fill an opening on the Commission with a former member. The Governor can, at the request of the Commission Chair pick a temporary substitute to fill an opening on the Commission or extend the term of a current member until a replacement is appointed. Only individuals who meet the constitutional eligibility requirements may be recalled or appointed to the Commission.
measures.no: A vote AGAINST the amendment means that current membership rules for the Commission stay the same. Temporary appointments are not allowed if a member is recused, disqualified, or if a member's term ends.
measures.r: To pass, the amendment needs more FOR votes than AGAINST votes among the votes cast on it. (Maryland Constitution, article XIV, section 1)

In Maryland an amendment is proposed by a bill passed by three-fifths of all the members elected to each house and then goes to the voters at the next general election (Maryland Constitution, article XIV, section 1); there is no citizen initiative for amendments.

measures.t: Executive Branch – Merit System - Binding Arbitration
measures.q:
To amend the Anne Arundel County Charter to permit all authorized employee representatives to enter into binding arbitration to resolve labor disputes relating to the terms and conditions of employment.
Currently, only authorized employee representatives of uniformed firefighters and uniformed officers of the County Police Department, Sheriff's Department, and Office of Detention Facilities may enter into binding arbitration with the County to resolve labor disputes relating to the terms and conditions of employment. There are several other labor organizations in the County that cannot enter into binding arbitration with the County.

measures.no: A vote AGAINST the charter amendment would retain the current binding arbitration provisions in the County Charter, meaning only authorized employee representatives of uniformed firefighters and uniformed officers of the County Police Department, Sheriff's Department, and Office of Detention Facilities may enter into binding arbitration to resolve labor disputes relating to the terms and conditions of employment.

This Charter Amendment establishes an Inspector General Appointment Board; provides for the appointment of members to the Appointment Board; provides authority for the Inspector General Appointment Board to appoint or reappoint the Inspector General and, if necessary, remove the Inspector General for cause. measures.t: LEGISLATION, BUDGET, AND BOARD OF ESTIMATES
measures.q:
Question F amends the City Charter's legislative process, the annual budget process, and the role of the Board of Estimates. It shortens the amount of time in which the Mayor can veto legislation passed by the City Council and the amount of time the City Council has to override the Mayor's veto.
The Amendment also eliminates the preliminary budget hearing process and transfers from the Board of Estimates to the Mayor the responsibility to prepare and submit the proposed budget before April 30 each year. The City Council must then adopt the budget at least eight days before the beginning of the fiscal year on July 1, and any veto and veto override process must be completed by then.
The Amendment removes the current $1 million dollar cap on the amount that may be used as a contingent fund for emergencies or other unexpected needs. It allows the Finance Director and the Planning Commission to make new recommendations about the proposed budget after it is submitted to the City Council and allows the City Council to add amounts based on those recommendations before final passage. The Amendment also transfers from the Board of Estimates to the Finance Director or the Planning Commission the authority to make supplemental appropriation recommendations outside of the annual budget process.
The Amendment transfers from the Board of Estimates to the Finance Department the responsibility to estimate revenues and formulate the annual rates for all property taxes, and transfers from the Board of Estimates to the Finance Director the responsibility to estimate any surpluses. It also transfers from the Board of Estimates to the Mayor the authority to increase or decrease the salaries of municipal officers in preparing the budget.
The Amendment removes from the Charter a number of other duties assigned to the Board of Estimates, including formulating and executing the fiscal policy of the City, advertising for contracts, establishing the process for professional services contracts and for bidder prequalification, approving emergency contracts, fixing salary and wage scales of employees, approving collective bargaining agreements, determining bonds of City officials, establishing procedures for paying or releasing claims against or claims held by the City, fixing the salary of officials in the State's Attorney's Office, and approving expenditures for new improvements. These roles could be given to other agencies or departments by City ordinance.
measures.y: Voting for this amendment brings about the changes described above, with the following effective dates: November 7, 2028, for Charter sections that are removed, unless an ordinance or regulation governing that topic is adopted sooner; December 5, 2028, for changes to approving and vetoing legislation; and December 3, 2026, for all other changes.
measures.no: Voting against the amendment leaves the current Charter language governing legislation, budget, and the Board of Estimates in place.
measures.r: To pass, the charter amendment needs more FOR votes than AGAINST votes among the votes cast on it; it then becomes part of the charter on the thirtieth day after the election. (Maryland Constitution, article XI-A, section 5)
measures.h: In Maryland a charter amendment is proposed by the council (in Baltimore, the Mayor and City Council) or by a petition of the registered voters, and goes to the voters at the next general election (Maryland Constitution, article XI-A, section 5). The State Board's list does not say which way this one came.

measures.q:
Question G amends the City Charter language governing how the City allows third parties to use certain City property. It adds the City's stormwater system to the list of City property that cannot be sold or rented out as a franchise. It clarifies that space in the City's conduit system can be rented out as a franchise, but the conduit system itself still cannot be sold. The Amendment also simplifies the general provisions governing franchise agreements and other such grants.
The Amendment updates the language for granting minor privileges to use a portion of City property by clarifying the definition of minor privilege, including temporary and permanent varieties, and permitting minor privileges to be further identified and defined by ordinance. It also removes the Board of Estimates' authority to grant minor privileges, along with related processes, and instead allows minor privileges to be granted by an executive agency under a new process to be established by City ordinance.
The Amendment also eliminates certain obsolete provisions in the Charter pertaining to street railways and trackless trolleys.

From those lists this site reads only the office, the district, the county and the city, town or district a contest belongs to, the candidate’s name, the party, the ballot order where the list gives one, and the primary vote counts. Addresses, phone numbers, e-mail and websites, where a list carries them, are never read, kept or shown. No photos, ages, biographies or campaign money are shown for state and local candidates.
lists

Parties. Offices elected on party lines show the party each candidate filed under, written out. Judges are on the nonpartisan ballot; the page says so instead of a party. Among the county and local contests here, county offices are elected on party lines; cities and school districts are nonpartisan. Each contest’s own page says which, from the list it was read from.
lists

Primaries. Where more people ran in a primary (June 23) than it could send on, everyone on that primary ballot is shown, with who went on to November, read from the general election list. Vote counts are the official results where they are loaded; where they are not, the race says so.
lists
Order. Candidates appear in the ballot order the list gives, or by surname where it gives none. Never by money, polls or party.
places
Places. A county or local contest is filed under every county or city it reaches. The names of cities, towns and districts come from the U.S. Census Bureau, each named among these sources.
holders

Who holds a seat today (the Legislature and the statewide offices the roster carries) comes from the Open States roster the record side of this site uses. A candidate matched to a sitting legislator by district and name, one fit only, links to their record page and nothing more.
maps

Maps and “use my location”. District lines are the Census Bureau’s cartographic boundary files (2024 Census Bureau cartographic boundary files), the lines the state pages draw, and the county lines are the Bureau’s too (2024 Census Bureau cartographic boundary file (counties, 1:500,000)); your county’s sample ballot is the authority on your district. Your location is worked out on your own device and never sent anywhere; a rounded copy (about half a mile) is kept on the device, with your choices, until you tap “Forget”. A typed address goes from your device straight to the U.S. Census Bureau’s address finder, only when you press Look up; only the spot it finds comes back, used the same way, and this site never sees or keeps the address.
page
Nobody is scored or graded. The cards show the record; the judging is yours.
polls

Polls of the statewide races are counted only from pollsters in the American Association for Public Opinion Research’s Transparency Initiative, who publish how each poll was done: the latest from up to five of them, each checked against the pollster’s own release, and our own average of the ten most recent, with the arithmetic shown. Published polls by other pollsters that we have checked against their own release are shown apart, under Other published polls, for reference, and are never counted in the average; the rest are counted and named. A poll is a measure of opinion when it was taken, with a margin of error, not a forecast.
polls

Betting markets. Prices on Polymarket, a prediction market, are shown for the statewide races it lists, as information only: not a poll, not a forecast and not an official record. They are read from its public data, and prices move all day. Where Kalshi or PredictIt (two other markets) lists a race, the page says so and links to it, but shows none of its prices: their terms do not allow other sites to show them. A notice comes before any link to a market. The Civic Archive takes no money from any market and uses no referral links.
lists

The contests for Congress at the top of your ballot are the Congress pages’ own, from the state’s official candidate list: each name as printed, with its party label, in the ballot order the list gives (or by surname where it gives none), with its write-in and incumbent marks. Everything else about those candidates is on their race’s Congress page. Your U.S. House district is found from the Census Bureau’s 119th Congress lines, the ones the Congress pages draw, on your own device.
rules

Ballot questions. Each question’s official texts are shown word for word: the question as it will be printed and, where the record has them, the official summary, what a yes and a no vote do and the fiscal note, each labelled by who wrote it where the record says, and by its source. Where this site puts something in its own words (often the votes needed to pass and how the question got on the ballot), the question’s page says so beside it. Each side’s arguments in the official voter guide are linked, never reprinted.
page

Your ballot, printed or kept. “As it will look” draws your ballot as a printed sample ballot; it is a preview, not an official ballot, and your county’s own sample ballot is the authority. “Keep this ballot on my phone” saves the contests, the names, the questions’ words and the names of your districts and places in this device’s own storage, with the date, to open with no signal. No location, no address and no account: nothing is sent anywhere. “Forget my location and choices” removes it, and so does “Forget this ballot” on the kept page. Anyone holding your unlocked phone can see which districts a kept ballot is for.

changelog.title: Top movers, and breaking-news alerts for Election Night
items: Top movers: a ticker on the Forecasts page, on Election Night's Forecasts page and on the front page shows the races whose forecast moved most since the previous day's, like a stock ticker: the state, the office, the leading candidate's chance and how many points it moved, and "now leads" where the lead changed hands. Each one opens the race's chart. It stops when you point at it or move to it with the keyboard, has a Pause button, and never moves for anyone who has Motion off, Calm on or reduced motion on their device: the races then sit in a row you can scroll. Labelled Analysis.

Election Night alerts: on the night (from 4 p.m. Central on November 3), a banner across the top of every page brings the news as it comes: polls closing in each state, each state's first official results, a race whose live forecast passes 95%, a new leader in the live forecast, and projections. An early projection comes when the model gives a candidate 99% or more with at least a quarter of the expected vote counted; a full projection, in a stronger brass band, from half counted. Each says how much is counted, is labelled Analysis and "as reported, not final", and the official count decides. A projection that stops holding is withdrawn in an alert of its own. Pause, See all alerts and Close are there; nothing makes a sound; before the night the pages ask for nothing.

changelog.title: Forecasts stamped with the date and time, newest polls, ballots cast
items: Every forecast now carries the date and time it was made, so you can follow how it moved. The forecast record keeps a copy each morning until November 2, and another whenever a new run of the model changes anything, each listed by the date and time it was taken; each race's small line follows its chance from one copy to the next.

Each race's chart marks the model's earlier runs with their date and time, placed by the hour on the time line. On the Forecasts page each race says when its forecast was made, and from the standard level up a small line shows how the leading candidate's chance moved, run by run; the top of the page says when the newest run was made.

Newest polls: new polls by members of the Transparency Initiative, each checked against the pollster's own release, add 19 race results to the averages: CNN's polls by SSRS in Kansas, Maine, Michigan and Texas (Senate and governor), Emerson in Kansas, ActiVote in Texas, East Carolina University in South Carolina, Concord in South Dakota and Montana, and High Point University in North Carolina (Senate and Supreme Court). 16 results by other pollsters, in Alaska, Alabama, Iowa, Michigan, Montana, South Carolina and Texas, are shown apart and never averaged. Polls we could not check against their own release (the New York Times/Siena polls of Minnesota and Florida, the Washington Post's of Kansas, Michigan State University's of Michigan) are listed as waiting, not shown. The poll finder no longer files a statewide poll under a House district.

Ballots cast so far: new counts from California, Colorado, Hawaii, Idaho, Maine, North Dakota, Oregon and Texas. South Dakota's newest weekly file is held back: one of its own totals does not match its party rows, so its page keeps the October 23 figures until the state corrects it.
The forecasts were made again with the new polls and counts.

changelog.title: Sandbox: Reading & access, in lanes
items: A second sandbox experiment, on the draft site only: the reading and access settings sorted into six lanes (Language, How much, Text, Colour and contrast, Motion and calm, Ready-made sets). Open a lane and its settings are tabs: click one to pin it open, as many as you like, and your pins are kept on this device. Open another lane and it opens to the left of the first, so several can be open at once; on a phone they line up in a strip you swipe through.
The Language lane comes first and names every language with a finished translation in its own words. Choosing one shows the page again in that language, with the lane still open.
The settings are the site's own, so whatever is chosen there carries to every page. Every other page still opens the usual panel.

changelog.title: Final-week polls, Texas specials, Connecticut's towns, Election Night readiness
items: Final-week polls: 32 more polls, each checked against the pollster's own release. Polls by members of the Transparency Initiative count in the averages: Marquette, Marist, Siena, Michigan State, Concord, Emerson, Targoz, ActiVote and the University of North Florida, across Senate and governor races in Wisconsin, Maine, New York, Michigan, Nebraska, Rhode Island, South Carolina and Florida, and U.S. House districts NY-17, WA-03 and KY-06. Polls by others are shown apart and never averaged; those paid for by a campaign or a party say so. Polls we could not check against their own release (the New York Times/Siena district polls, Emerson's subscriber-only district polls) are listed as waiting, not shown. The day's forecasts were made again with them.

Texas: the state's November 3 special elections for State House District 93 and State Senate District 22, the 276th District Court, a Democrat added to one judicial race, and nine declared write-ins are now on Texas's ballot pages, from the Secretary of State's own lists.

Connecticut: every town has now posted its sample ballot, and all are read: registrars of voters, town and school board contests, and every probate district now carry their candidates (110 local races, up from 76).

On state ballot pages, 43 kinds of local office that were listed at the end under their own titles (Florida's community development boards, library boards, receivers of taxes and others) now sit with the offices like them.

Election Night: Minnesota's saved results files are read about four times faster; Texas's two special elections and its judicial race are tied to the state's results; a new check holds back any state's file that shows votes before its polls close (three states' test files do today); and practice runs can no longer reach the public results.
Election Night counts 267 statewide races, and the U.S. page now names the District of Columbia's two offices apart from them. The Past results door now says all 50 states and DC are loaded.

State ballot pages: Georgia's and Virginia's mail-ballot notes no longer call October 23 "this Friday"; notes and source lines no longer describe how this site reads its files or show raw web addresses (each source's link is still there).

Wording: the news-outlet count now matches everywhere; the Method page says plainly that polls outside our average are shown apart; it says which Forecasts page lists every forecast; the privacy answers now name the Forecasts page's address look-up and street maps, and the Access page names the weather picture's one request; the page guide no longer says Minnesota is the only state with a forecast map.

changelog.title: A sandbox, and Anthropic's prospectus four ways
items: A sandbox on the draft site, for experiments: in no menu, not on the live site, and every page asks search engines not to list it.

Its first experiment is the prospectus Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, filed with the SEC on October 26, 2026, four ways. As filed: a link to the official copy on SEC.gov. In chapters: save the official copy from SEC.gov and open it in a reader that rebuilds it into its 27 chapters, with highlights, notes, search, a page-by-page view as filed, and a PDF of a chapter, the chapters you marked, your notes alone or the whole filing. The copy and your notes stay on your device; this site never holds the filing's text. In five minutes: about 1,230 words in the filing's own order, in our words, checked claim by claim against the filing. And an analysis of whether it reads as if an AI wrote it: whether text carries a mark that says so (it does not, for anyone to read), and the word counts studies tie to AI writing, beside eight other prospectuses, four of them filed before ChatGPT existed. Every figure there is labelled Analysis and says what it cannot tell you.
The pages say the site is built with the help of Claude, and that Anthropic had no part in them.

Ballots cast so far: California, South Dakota, Colorado, Louisiana, Oregon and South Carolina are current again, read from the new names and layouts their offices now use. Iowa's site now refuses programs and Washington shows its counts only inside a dashboard, so both wait for a hand-saved copy; Oklahoma has not posted yet. Building these pages takes under a second, down from half an hour.

changelog.title: Every state on the forecast map
items: Each state on both Forecasts pages now has its map and "Your ballot, as forecast", with Share: all 40 states with a forecast, not Minnesota alone. Use your location or type your address, and the page lists every race on your ballot there with the model's forecast where it has one. Your location stays on your device.
A state's map and its list of races load only when you open that state.
In the states that drew new congressional lines for 2026, the map says so, and your U.S. House district is found only from the new lines, never the old ones.

The nine states with new U.S. House districts for 2026 (Alabama, California, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee, Texas, Utah) now show those districts on the ballot maps, from the Census Bureau's 2026 plan files published October 6, and "Use my location" or a typed address finds your 2026 district there. Before, those maps showed only the state's outline.

A statewide board elected by district (Texas's State Board of Education and others) is no longer put on every ballot in the state: it is placed by its own district, or the page says it cannot tell which seat is yours.
Past results load from the site's own results store rather than from each copy of the site, which leaves more room for election week.

Where a state's precinct lines are not on file here, your ballot still lists its statewide races. A statewide board elected by district (a state board of education, a public service commission) is no longer put on every ballot in the state: it is counted among the races the page could not place, and the state's own ballot lookup is the authority.

_retention.t: In a retention vote the judge has no opponent: you vote yes or no on keeping the judge. The yes share needed differs by state, such as 60 percent in Illinois and 57 percent in New Mexico.
s: Frequently Asked Questions About Retention, Alaska Judicial Council
2026 retention recommendations, New Mexico Judicial Performance Evaluation Commission
Illinois Constitution, Article VI, Section 12 (Election and retention), Illinois General Assembly

x.es: En un voto de retención, el juez no tiene contrincante: usted vota sí o no a que el juez continúe en el cargo. La proporción de votos por el sí que se necesita varía según el estado; por ejemplo, 60 por ciento en Illinois y 57 por ciento en Nuevo México.

attorney_general.t: The attorney general is the state's top lawyer. The office speaks for the state in court, advises state agencies and enforces consumer laws.
s: About Our Office, Minnesota Attorney General
About the Office of Attorney General, Arizona Attorney General

x.es: El procurador general es el principal abogado del estado. La oficina representa al estado ante los tribunales, asesora a las agencias estatales y hace cumplir las leyes de protección al consumidor.

circuit_court.t: In most states that have them, circuit courts are the main trial courts, for serious crimes, big lawsuits and often divorce. In Wyoming the circuit court is a lower court for smaller cases.
s: Florida's Court Structure (Annual Report 2018-19), Florida State Courts
How Cases Proceed Through the Courts, Illinois Courts
About the Courts, Kentucky Court of Justice
Michigan Compiled Laws 600.601 (circuit court jurisdiction), Michigan Legislature

x.es: En la mayoría de los estados que los tienen, los tribunales de circuito son los principales tribunales de primera instancia, para delitos graves, demandas grandes y, a menudo, divorcios. En Wyoming, el tribunal de circuito es un tribunal inferior para casos más pequeños.

clerk_of_court.t: The clerk of court keeps trial court records, takes in filings and collects fines and fees. In North Carolina the clerk also handles estates, and in Florida, county records and money.
s: North Carolina General Statutes 28A-2-1 (clerk of superior court, probate of wills and estates), North Carolina General Assembly
North Carolina General Statutes 7A-103 (powers of the clerk of superior court), North Carolina General Assembly
Constitution of the State of Florida, Florida Legislature (Online Sunshine)

x.es: El secretario del tribunal lleva los registros de los tribunales de primera instancia, recibe los documentos que se presentan y cobra multas y tarifas. En Carolina del Norte, el secretario también se encarga de las herencias y, en Florida, de los registros y el dinero del condado.

comptroller.t: The comptroller is a top money officer, and the job differs by state. It can mean paying the state's bills, running its pension fund or collecting its taxes.
s: About Us, Connecticut Office of the State Comptroller
About the New York State Comptroller's Office
What does the agency do?, Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
The Role of the Comptroller, Comptroller of Maryland
Illinois Constitution, Article V, Section 17 (Comptroller - duties), Illinois General Assembly
About Us, South Carolina Comptroller General

x.es: El contralor es uno de los principales funcionarios encargados del dinero, y el trabajo varía según el estado. Puede consistir en pagar las cuentas del estado, administrar su fondo de pensiones o cobrar sus impuestos.

council.t: The city or town council makes the city's laws. It also passes the budget and sets taxes and fees.
s: Kentucky Municipal Statutory Law, Informational Bulletin No. 145, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission
State and Local Government, Chapter 3 Part A: Local Government, Louisiana House of Representatives

x.es: El concejo de la ciudad o del pueblo hace las leyes de la ciudad. También aprueba el presupuesto y fija los impuestos y las tarifas.

county_attorney.t: The county attorney brings criminal cases in county courts and is also the lawyer for county government. In some states this office is called the state's attorney.
s: Duties of Elected County Officials, Informational Bulletin No. 114, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission
Texas Constitution, Article 5 (Judicial Department), Texas Legislature

x.es: El abogado del condado presenta casos penales en los tribunales del condado y también es el abogado del gobierno del condado. En algunos estados, este cargo se llama fiscal del estado.

county_commissioner.t: The county's governing board passes the budget, sets taxes and oversees services like roads. Its members are called commissioners, and in some places supervisors or police jurors.
s: North Dakota Century Code chapter 11-11, Board of County Commissioners, North Dakota Legislative Branch
State and Local Government, Chapter 3 Part A: Local Government, Louisiana House of Representatives

x.es: La junta de gobierno del condado aprueba el presupuesto, fija los impuestos y supervisa servicios como los caminos. Sus miembros se llaman comisionados y, en algunos lugares, supervisores o jurados de policía.

county_council.t: The county council makes the county's laws. A separate elected executive or mayor runs the county's departments.
s: Maryland at a Glance: Government (Charter counties), Maryland Manual, Maryland State Archives
Maryland Constitution, Article XI-A, Maryland State Archives

x.es: El concejo del condado hace las leyes del condado. Un ejecutivo o un alcalde elegido por separado dirige los departamentos del condado.

county_executive.t: This office runs the county's offices, while a separate elected council makes the laws. In Kentucky the county judge/executive also leads the county board.
s: Maryland at a Glance: Government (Charter counties), Maryland Manual, Maryland State Archives
Duties of Elected County Officials, Informational Bulletin No. 114, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission

x.es: Este cargo dirige las oficinas del condado, mientras que un concejo elegido por separado hace las leyes. En Kentucky, el juez/ejecutivo del condado también dirige la junta del condado.

county_treasurer.t: The county treasurer collects property taxes and keeps the county's money safe. The office shares it with schools, cities and other districts, but does not set how much is owed.
s: North Dakota Century Code chapter 11-14, County Treasurer, North Dakota Legislative Branch
Minnesota Statutes chapter 385, County Treasurer, Minnesota Revisor of Statutes

x.es: El tesorero del condado cobra los impuestos sobre la propiedad y guarda de forma segura el dinero del condado. La oficina lo reparte entre escuelas, ciudades y otros distritos, pero no decide cuánto se debe.

court_of_appeals.t: The court of appeals is the middle level of state courts. Its judges check trial court rulings for legal mistakes when one side appeals, and they do not hold new trials.
s: Florida's Court Structure (Annual Report 2018-19), Florida State Courts
How courts work, California Courts Self-Help Center
About the Courts, Kentucky Court of Justice

x.es: El tribunal de apelaciones es el nivel intermedio de los tribunales del estado. Cuando una de las partes apela, sus jueces revisan si las decisiones de los tribunales de primera instancia tienen errores legales, y no celebran juicios nuevos.

governor.t: The governor is the state's top leader. The governor signs or vetoes new laws, names many state officials and leads the state's military forces.
s: Texas Constitution, Article 4 (Executive Department), Texas Legislature
Michigan Constitution of 1963, Article V (Executive Branch), Michigan Legislature

x.es: El gobernador es el líder principal del estado. El gobernador firma o veta las nuevas leyes, nombra a muchos funcionarios estatales y dirige las fuerzas militares del estado.

mayor.t: The mayor is the city's elected leader and, in some cities, runs city departments. Where the council hires a city manager, the mayor leads the council and the manager does the daily work.
s: Kentucky Municipal Statutory Law, Informational Bulletin No. 145, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission
State and Local Government, Chapter 3 Part A: Local Government, Louisiana House of Representatives

x.es: El alcalde es el líder elegido de la ciudad y, en algunas ciudades, dirige los departamentos municipales. Donde el concejo contrata a un administrador municipal, el alcalde dirige el concejo y el administrador hace el trabajo diario.

orphans_court.t: Despite its name, Maryland's Orphans' Court is the county's probate court. Its judges oversee the estates of people who have died and guardianship of children's property.

x.es: A pesar de su nombre, el Tribunal de Huérfanos de Maryland es el tribunal de sucesiones del condado. Sus jueces supervisan los bienes de las personas fallecidas y la tutela de los bienes de los niños.

register_of_wills.t: The register of wills handles the paperwork after someone dies. It takes in wills and names who settles the estate, and in Maryland it collects inheritance taxes.
s: Frequently Asked Questions, Maryland Register of Wills
Delaware Code Title 12, Chapter 25, Register of Wills, Delaware General Assembly

x.es: El registrador de testamentos se encarga de los trámites después de que alguien muere. Recibe los testamentos y nombra a quien liquida la herencia y, en Maryland, cobra los impuestos sobre la herencia.

school_board.t: The school board runs a public school district. It hires the superintendent, sets district rules, passes the budget and, in many states, sets the local school tax.
s: Statutory Requirements for School Districts, Informational Paper 29 (Wisconsin Legislative Fiscal Bureau), Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction
Board of Education, Mercer County Schools, Kentucky
SBDM Councils & School Board Duties, Oldham County Schools, Kentucky

x.es: La junta escolar dirige un distrito escolar público. Contrata al superintendente, fija las reglas del distrito, aprueba el presupuesto y, en muchos estados, fija el impuesto escolar local.

sheriff.t: In most states the sheriff is the county's top law officer. The office keeps the peace, runs the jail and carries out court orders; in Kentucky it also collects property taxes.
s: Minnesota Statutes 387.03, Powers, duties, Minnesota Revisor of Statutes
Minnesota Statutes 387.11, County jail, Minnesota Revisor of Statutes
Duties of Elected County Officials, Informational Bulletin No. 114, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission

x.es: En la mayoría de los estados, el alguacil es el principal agente de la ley del condado. La oficina mantiene la paz, dirige la cárcel y cumple las órdenes de los tribunales; en Kentucky, también cobra los impuestos sobre la propiedad.

state_house.t: The state House (called the Assembly or House of Delegates in some states) is the larger chamber. Its members write and vote on state laws and the state budget.
s: What is the Legislature?, Wisconsin State Legislature
Legislative Q&A, Colorado House of Representatives

state_senate.t: The state Senate is the smaller of the Legislature's two chambers (Nebraska has only one). Senators write and vote on state laws and the state budget.
s: What is the Legislature?, Wisconsin State Legislature
Legislative Branch Function and Process, North Dakota Legislative Branch

x.es: El Senado estatal es la más pequeña de las dos cámaras de la Legislatura (Nebraska tiene solo una). Los senadores redactan y votan las leyes estatales y el presupuesto del estado.

supreme_court.t: The state supreme court is the state's highest court. It hears appeals from lower courts and has the final say on state law (Texas also has a top court for criminal cases).
s: Texas Courts: A Descriptive Summary, Texas Judicial Branch
Court System Information, Alaska Court System
About the Courts, Kentucky Court of Justice
Judicial System Structure, Supreme Court of Ohio

x.es: La corte suprema del estado es el tribunal más alto del estado. Atiende apelaciones de los tribunales inferiores y tiene la última palabra sobre la ley estatal (Texas también tiene un tribunal máximo para los casos penales).
